#6650. Pumpkin Cheesecake Muffins

Loaded with pumpkin seeds, canned pumpkin purée, and pumpkin pie spice, these big streusel-topped muffins are every fall lover’s dream come true. And to make things even better, the inside of each muffin is stuffed with a soft, lightly sweetened cream cheese mixture. Make the cheesecake filling and the streusel ahead of time to pace things out if it’s helpful. Don’t, even for a minute, consider using anything other than Libby’s 100% pure pumpkin purée (not pie mix). Nothing is better. We promise.

This recipe is part of Pumpkin Week 2026, Bon Appétit’s annual celebration of autumn’s most magical pantry staple.

Whisk ⅓ cup coarsely chopped raw pumpkin seeds, ¼ cup (31 g) all-purpose flour, 2 Tbsp. light brown sugar, ½ tsp. pumpkin pie spice, and a pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl to combine. Using your fingers, rub in 2 Tbsp. unsalted butter, room temperature, until moist pea-size lumps form. Chill until ready to use.

Do Ahead: Streusel can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and keep chilled.

Vigorously whisk 6 oz. cream cheese, room temperature, ¼ cup (50 g) granulated sugar, 2 tsp. all-purpose flour, 2 tsp. vanilla extract, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl until combined and smooth.

Do Ahead: Filling can be made 1 day ahead. Cover and chill.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 375°. Line cups of a standard 12-cup muffin pan with paper liners. Whisk 2 large eggs, 1½ cups (packed; 300 g) light brown sugar, 1 cup canned pumpkin purée, ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, ¼ cup whole milk, 1 Tbsp. pumpkin pie spice, 1 Tbsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1 tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth, about 1 minute. Whisk 1¾ cups (219 g) all-purpose flour and 1½ tsp. baking powder in a small bowl to combine. Add to pumpkin mixture and fold in with a rubber spatula until just incorporated and no large dry streaks of flour remain (don’t overmix; batter will be lumpy).

Bake muffins until streusel is crisp and muffins spring back when gently pressed, 24–27 minutes. Let muffins cool in pan 5 minutes, then turn out onto a wire rack and let cool until just warm or completely.

Do Ahead: Muffins can be made 2 days ahead. Store airtight at room temperature.

#6648. How to Moisturize Your Scalp in 6 Easy Steps

Whenever my scalp feels tight and itchy and I notice white flakes falling, I wonder whether my love of hot showers (yes, I’m guilty of turning my small NYC shower into the equivalent of a hot spring) or my daily use of hot styling tools might be contributing. Whatever the cause, I know it’s time to give my scalp some extra attention.

As Hadley King, MD, a New York City board-certified dermatologist, explains, dry skin is generally characterized by water loss and a disrupted skin barrier. The same applies to the scalp, which Dr. King says needs both water-binding ingredients and barrier-supporting lipids to stay moisturized.

Several things can cause a dry scalp. Morgan Rabach, MD, a board-certified dermatologist and cofounder of LM Medical NYC, lists overwashing, using hot water in the shower, excessive hot tool use, and overprocessing hair with harsh chemicals as habits that may contribute. Certain skin conditions, like eczema or seborrheic dermatitis, and environmental factors such as cold weather or low humidity are also common causes.

Additionally, Y. Claire Chang, MD, a board-certified dermatologist at UnionDerm, adds that sebum production can decrease with age and during hormonal changes, making your scalp even more prone to dryness. These are all things you’ll want to address because, as we know, healthy hair comes from a healthy scalp. “The scalp is an extension of the skin on the face and body,” says Dr. Chang. “It is important to maintain a healthy skin barrier on the scalp just like the rest of the body.”

Luckily, it’s not too hard to keep your scalp moisturized. Just consider adding the following steps to your routine.

The first step to moisturizing your scalp is washing it with a gentle shampoo formulated with hydrating ingredients like glycerin, ceramides, and hyaluronic acid. Dr. King agrees and recommends using a gentle, non-medicated shampoo rather than a harsher clarifying shampoo if the scalp is dry. “The goal is to remove sweat, sebum, and product buildup without stripping the scalp’s protective lipids,” she says.

She says to look for gentle surfactants and recommends a shampoo like the Nutrire S.1 Calm Shampoo for Dry Scalp, which contains humectants like glycerin and panthenol to retain water and watermelon seed oil to provide emollient lipids that smooth dry skin. Alexis Stephens, DO, a board-certified dermatologist based in Coral Springs, Florida, likes the Vanicream Shampoo for Sensitive Skin as it is made without several of the most common irritants found in products, such as fragrance and essential oils. “It’s a good option for people with sensitive scalps or those who experience irritation from fragranced hair products,” Dr. Stephens says. “While it isn’t a moisturizer itself, it helps establish a gentler cleansing routine that supports scalp comfort.”

Like your face, your scalp skin can get dry when you overdo exfoliation. “A dry scalp generally doesn’t need aggressive scrubbing,” Dr. King says. “If someone has significant scale, it’s important to determine whether we’re dealing with seborrheic dermatitis or psoriasis rather than simply trying to exfoliate it away.”

After shampooing, Dr. Chang recommends using a moisturizing scalp treatment. Look for nourishing ingredients like hyaluronic acid, glycerin, or panthenol for that added moisture. You’ll want to part your hair into sections to apply the product directly to the scalp, she says, and she recommends something like the Kérastase Nutritive Hydrating Scalp Serum; it’s a lightweight leave-in treatment made with plant-based proteins, glycerin, panthenol, and niacinamide to provide targeted hydration. Dr. King likes The Ordinary Natural Moisturizing Factors + HA for Scalp, which she says is packed with moisturizing factors that replicate components naturally found in skin to help keep the skin hydrated.

Conditioning your hair is still an important part of your routine, particularly if you’re experiencing dryness along the hair shaft as well as on your scalp. Dr. Stephens says this is especially important for curly and coily hair textures, which may need more conditioning along the hair shaft even when the scalp itself isn’t dry. She likes the CeraVe Gentle Hydrating Conditioner, which contains known hydrating ingredients such as hyaluronic acid, niacinamide, and glycerin to support the skin barrier. “It’s also suitable for all curl patterns, including curly and coily hair, and helps leave the hair feeling softer and more manageable after cleansing,” she says.

Dr. Chang recommends applying conditioner primarily to the midlengths and ends to keep hair hydrated and to reduce breakage. We like the Nécessaire The Conditioner, as it’s fragrance-free and made with nourishing ingredients like glycerin, ceramides, and hyaluronic acid to keep hair hydrated and healthy.

Environmental stressors like the sun’s harmful UV rays can exacerbate dryness, which is why Dr. Chang encourages patients to use proper sun protection, such as hats and scalp-friendly sunscreen (we like the Sun Bum SPF 30 Sunscreen Scalp and Hair Mist Spray or the Coola Scalp Hair Spray Sunscreen SPF 30 Mist) on exposed areas. This is particularly important for anyone with thinning hair or a visible scalp.

Though it can feel soothing, Dr. Chang says to avoid washing your hair in excessively hot water, as it can dry out your scalp. Instead, use lukewarm water and keep your showers short to avoid stripping your scalp of its natural oils.

You’ll also want to avoid excessive product buildup, as heavy oils, dry shampoos, and styling products can accumulate on the scalp and potentially contribute to irritation. Regular cleansing will be key, so use the right water temperature.

Anyone can experience a dry scalp, regardless of skin tone, skin type, or hair texture, Dr. Stephens says. But people with sensitive skin, eczema, or a history of contact dermatitis may be more susceptible. Dr. Chang adds that lifestyle and environmental factors (think cold weather, low humidity, and indoor heating during the winter), as well as age, can play a role.

What Is the Difference Between Dry Scalp and Dry Hair?

Distinguishing between dry scalp and dry hair matters when you’re trying to find the best products to address each concern. “One of the biggest misconceptions I see, particularly among patients with curly and coily hair, is that dry hair automatically means dry scalp,” Dr. Stephens says. “It doesn’t. Tightly coiled hair is more prone to dryness along the hair shaft, partly because natural scalp oils don’t distribute as easily down the curls. But the scalp underneath may be perfectly balanced or even oily. That’s why I encourage people to think of their scalp and hair as two areas with different needs.”

Dr. Chang says to think of it like this: Hair dryness is about how moisture and natural oils travel along the hair shaft, while scalp dryness is more closely related to skin barrier function, sebum production, underlying skin conditions, and environmental exposures.

What Ingredients Should You Avoid to Prevent a Dry Scalp?

Dr. Rabach lists hair dyes, fragrance, and certain alcohols as common culprits that can dry out the scalp and may be worth avoiding. Dr. Stephens agrees and adds that harsh cleansing formulas with alcohol can strip away too much of your scalp’s protective surface (especially when used too frequently) and can be drying or irritating.

Other ingredients to look out for, she says, are essential oils. “They don’t necessarily dry out the scalp directly, but they can trigger irritation or allergic contact dermatitis, which may leave the scalp feeling tight, itchy, or uncomfortable,” she says.

With ingredients like salicylic acid, which help with scalp issues such as dandruff, you still want to be careful, as they may worsen dryness if you use them too often. She adds that just because something is labeled “sulfate-free,” it doesn’t automatically mean it's gentle. You want to consider the formulation as a whole. “It’s important to remember that the overall formulation matters more than any single ingredient,” she says.

What Is the Difference Between Dry Scalp and Dandruff?

Dr. Chang says flaking doesn’t always mean your scalp is dry. Dandruff is generally considered a mild form of seborrheic dermatitis, a condition associated with Malassezia yeast, scalp oils, and inflammation. You’ll need a special type of treatment for these scalp conditions, and it’s best to consult your dermatologist for a proper diagnosis.

Dr. King adds that if you’re experiencing persistent itching, redness, thick scales, crusting, significant flaking, or any pain, it may be time to seek professional help. “I’d recommend evaluation rather than assuming it’s simple dryness,” she says.

When we test and review a product, we take a holistic approach to deliver well-rounded product recommendations. First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity estheticians—to gain professional insight into the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

For scalp moisturizing products, we selected the best based on ingredients, texture, ease of application, finish, and the hair-care concerns they address. To do this, we paired our personal tests of each formula with expert guidance and reviewer insights to determine what we would recommend. Read more about our testing methodology here.

#6647. Farmers Market Salad With Miso Maple Dressing

Most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

The farmers market is my biggest hack for solo cooking. Instead of committing to a three-pound bag of carrots, you can buy just one, and choose your produce based on beauty or mere curiosity. That’s how I came up with this fall salad, comprising a single head of Little Gem lettuce and some crunchy produce, including that carrot we mentioned, cucumber, watermelon radish, and an Asian pear. Slicing those elements thinly with a mandoline and throwing them in an ice bath for a brief soak helps keep everything cold and crisp.

The dressing is equally important. I start with Kewpie mayo for its richness and savory depth—it’s made with only egg yolks and contains MSG, giving it a fuller flavor than standard mayonnaise. White miso brings even more umami, while rice vinegar keeps things bright. The result is a creamy finger-licking dressing that clings to every bite. Serve with a fried egg (or your protein of choice) and a piece of fresh bread to scoop up the leftovers. Make a double batch of dressing for dipping crudités or marinating salmon, chicken, or roasted vegetables.

Read More: The Farmers Market Is Built for Solo Cooking

Combine 1 small head of Little Gem or other crunchy lettuce, leaves separated, cut into 2"–3" pieces, 1 rainbow carrot, peeled, very thinly sliced lengthwise into ribbons with a mandoline or vegetable peeler, 1 Persian cucumber, thinly sliced, preferably with a mandoline, ½ small watermelon radish, peeled, halved, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, and ¼ medium Asian pear, thinly sliced into half-moons, preferably with a mandoline, in a large bowl of ice water. Let soak 10–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk ¼ cup extra-virgin olive oil, 2 Tbsp. seasoned rice vinegar, 2 Tbsp. white miso, 2 tsp. Kewpie mayonnaise, 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, and 1 tsp. toasted sesame oil in a small bowl until smooth and emulsified (or combine in a small glass jar, cover, and shake). Taste dressing and season with kosher salt.

Drain vegetables and run through a salad spinner or pat dry with a kitchen towel to remove excess water. Wipe out large bowl, return vegetables to bowl, and drizzle 2 Tbsp. dressing over. Toss, adding more dressing as needed, until evenly coated (reserve any remaining dressing for another use).

Transfer salad to a shallow bowl or rimmed plate. Top with a fried egg and serve with country-style bread if desired.

Do Ahead: Dressing can be made up to 3 days ahead. Cover and chill.

#6646. Cider Braised Pork Shoulder

Pork and apples have been partners in crime since the beginning of time. Or at least, since the beginning of recorded recipe history. There’s something magical about how an apple’s natural sweetness and tartness can cut through a fatty, savory piece of pork, especially on a chilly fall day. Braising is by far one of my favorite fall cooking techniques, so after trying Food Editor Makinze’s apple cider braised brisket, I knew it was time to put my own spin on it with the apple’s natural bestie—pork shoulder.

The braise:Just like any good braise, this one starts with a quick sear in a Dutch oven to develop color and flavor on the exterior of the meat and activate the heat in the cayenne-pepper-dusted surface. Then, sliced red onions are seared in the pork fat along with garlic and my secret ingredient: fresh chopped ginger. The ginger brings a floral heat that complements both pork and the apples without overpowering the braising liquid. Once the onions cook down a little bit, the pork returns to the pot with apple cider and braises in a hot oven with fresh Granny Smith apple slices until it's practically falling apart.

How to serve:Shred the pork and serve it with cheesy grits, roasted potatoes, or spiced rice pilaf to make your new favorite, shareable fall dinner.

Make ahead & storage:Pork can be made 3 days ahead. Store in an airtight container and refrigerate.

#6645. Our 11 Favorite Watches Coming to the Biggest Auctions of the Year

Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

This is the biggest weekend of the year for vintage watches. It’s the year-end watch auctions in Geneva, where many prestigious houses bring their very best pieces to market. And it’s never been a more enthralling time to keep a close eye on what happens in Geneva over the next few days. In the first half of the year, the number of million-dollar watches nearly eclipsed the total for the entirety of 2025. A couple of the pieces listed below, including a unique Rolex and a rare Patek Philippe in stainless steel, have estimates above a million bucks.

Writer Oren Hartov and I pored over hundreds of lots to bring you our 11 favorite watches plus one bonus selection. See them all below.

You know a banger is coming up for sale when the house behind it doesn’t even bother capping its price range. Auction estimates are routinely and famously low to encourage bidders, and this watch’s starting point is still $1.2 million. Why? Well, have you ever seen a Rolex like this before? Before Rolex defined the look of modern watches with pieces like the Submariner, it operated similarly to many other manufacturers in Switzerland, willing to make one-off pieces and experiment frequently with its design.

This square beauty from the early 1940s is “most probably unique,” as Phillips auction house writes in its essay on the piece. This exact piece last hit the auction block in 2004, and no other example has come up for public sale since. It’s crazy to see how much this watch’s case shape resembles Heuer’s similarly blocky Monaco, which wouldn’t be released for another 25-plus years. Unfortunately, as cool as this watch is, it does not come with onyx prayer beads. —Cam Wolf

There’s Patek, then there’s complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples, then there’s stainless steel complicated Patek made in just a handful of examples in insane condition. This watch checks all those boxes. A reference 1436, it’s a split-seconds (rattrapante) chronograph, meaning it can time successive intervals of a race or event. One of just two stainless steel examples known to the market, it has an estimate of $2.4-$4.8M, a testament to its rarity and importance. —Oren Hartov

Yet another rare watch executed in stainless steel, this fabulous Lange 1 boasts a gorgeous two-tone dial in blue, with darker subdials contrasting against a cobalt-colored main dial. Dating to 1999 and first sold by the German retailer Oeding-Erdel, it’s one of approximately 30 pieces made in the most utilitarian of metals. Originally fitted with a more standard silvered dial, it received its current navy-blue dial as a replacement and is one of just two stainless steel Lange 1s known in this particular configuration. —OH

Renewed interest in Urban Jürgensen stemming from its recent relaunch under the directorship of Kari Voutilainen, who has since left the CEO position but remains on the company’s board, has seen watches such as this early-’90s ref. 2 garner more attention. A lovely perpetual calendar-moonphase, it’s housed in a classically inspired 37.7mm yellow gold case with cornes-de-vache-style lugs, a stepped bezel, and an incredible dial with the brand’s signature observatory-style hands. Someone tell Timothée Chalamet. —OH

Chopard has a hard-earned reputation for putting out some of the most finely made watches in Switzerland. It’s not just the nerds who are familiar with its work anymore, either. If we (the nerds, obviously) were sending a watch in a bottle to help share that message far and wide, this Lunar One, which looks like something out of Superman’s icy Fortress of Solitude, wouldn’t be a bad choice. This is Chopard’s first watch to combine a perpetual calendar and a moonphase, which is like shaving truffles on caviar. I love that the Roman numerals at 4 and 8 o’clock look like columns nearly buckling under the weight of the center of the dial. This watch also comes with several fun add-ons, like onyx prayer beads plus a ring and a pen set with diamonds. —Cam Wolf

While many younger collectors are obsessed with the Cosmograph Daytona, true “Crown” heads know that other pre-Daytona chronographs sometimes present an even more compelling proposition. This ref. 3525 ‘’Bariletto,’ dating to the 1940s, is not only the first Oyster-cased Rolex chronograph, but it’s also the only known stainless-steel example carrying the signature on the dial of Proud’s, a Rolex retailer based in Sydney. Manually wound, paired to a handsome beads-of-rice bracelet, and measuring a compact 36mm, it comes from the collection of important Italian collector Pucci Papaleo. —OH

While this stainless steel Patek may look like a normal ref. 2509—a beautiful hand-wound dress watch from the midcentury—it’s actually a “school watch” modified by a watchmaking student at the Geneva Watchmaking School. Dating to the 1960s, it’s housed in a 35mm stainless steel case and features a lovely dial with the ‘Ecole d’Horlogerie Geneve’ signature instead of Patek Philippe’s. Open it up, and the hand-wound movement is signed by Norbert Henry, the watchmaking student who assembled and finished it. While it may not attract the attention of more typical Patek collectors, its under-the-radar qualities make it a potential sleeper hit. —OH

It’s tough to argue with the sheer beauty of Vacheron’s mid-20th-century output, much of which is vastly underappreciated compared to comparable pieces from the likes of Patek Philippe. This splendid yellow gold ref. 4072 with a two-tone multi-scale dial dates to the late 1940s—one of my favorite eras of watch design. Powered by the hand-wound cal. V 492 movement and featuring a lovely set of long, contoured lugs, its dial is in fantastic condition, with applied dart and Roman indices, sharp printing, a crisp signature, and legible tachymeter and telemeter scales. It will surely find its way onto the wrist of a collector with excellent taste. —OH

This watch’s dial depicts Saint George, who, according to legend, slew a dragon while on horseback. This is a perfect use for the rich, deep colors you get from enamel. The flames licking at Saint George are beautiful shades of orange and red. He triumphantly lifts his spear as his steed rears its front legs. It’s very cool how much story you can get from this little 35mm timepiece. —CW

Watch collectors might pony up a few thousand for one of independent watchmaker F.P. Journe’s used tissues at this point. However, they’ll have to settle for a host of accessories coming to auction instead this weekend. The maker is so in-demand that, in addition to his timepieces, houses are selling his empty watch boxes and a set of toys that resemble him. This lot is in the middle of those two extremes: a wall clock made to resemble Journe’s Octa Réserve de Marche. Although I’m not gonna lie, flipping this over and seeing the compartment where you stuff in the batteries is a bit of a buzzkill. —CW

They used to make everything look more elegant. This original Longines design was developed in 1931 with famous aviator Charles Lindbergh. It is technically a pilot’s watch, but its elegant, icy-blue dial and Roman numerals would make it the fanciest model on many red carpets in 2026. This is a model from the ‘80s inspired by that original design, and it comes on an absolutely righteous beads-of-rice bracelet. Someone is going to get this guy for around $2,500 if the estimate is correct! —CW

In Rolex world, even the advertisements sell for thousands of dollars. It’s hard to blame people when we’re talking about a rare poster of a GMT-Master wearing a snow-dusted Rolex beanie. Awwww. (Relatedly, imagine if Rolex sold that beanie!? Oh, boy.) —CW

#6644. From Rihanna to Rosalía, These Are Martine Rose’s Biggest Celebrity Superfans

At last, the news has officially broken: Martine Rose has been appointed to the helm of Balenciaga. While expectations of the announcement have been brewing for the past few months, it’s one that has been met with pretty much ubiquitous celebration.

That’s not to dismiss the achievements of her predecessor, Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose tenure was marked by a sculptural, romantic flair and a rich sense for color and textural play. Still, the warmth expressed for the British designer’s appointment is uniquely multifaceted. There’s its representational significance, as she joins a growing coterie of women of color at the helm of fashion’s most influential houses, but beyond that—and arguably more importantly—is her skill as a designer, and its capacity to shape the fashion conversation at large.

That’s something she’s more than proved at her namesake label, where her tweaked-and-twisted, often quietly kinky riffs on the everyday dress codes she observes in her native London have been key in bridging the gap between the realms of streetwear and high fashion over the past decade. There is also, as anyone versed in their menswear lore will know, the fact that Rose’s big break arguably came at Balenciaga, where she played an instrumental role in shaping the aesthetic of the house, working alongside Demna during the early, agenda-setting years of his tenure. And then, as we’ve come to know over the years, there’s Martine Rose herself: one of the sharpest and funniest voices the industry has in its midst.

You don’t have to look far for proof of just how widely her influence has spread. Though often framed as something of a fashion insider’s favorite, Rose has an equally devoted A-list following. Rihanna is regularly spotted in her designs, while Kendrick Lamar has all but appointed her his de facto dresser for some of the biggest moments of his career, wearing custom Rose looks to collect his Best Rap Album Grammy in 2023 and for his critically acclaimed 2025 Super Bowl half-time performance.

Below, revisit the moments your favorite celebrities repped one of fashion’s favorite designers.

In October 2025, Justin Bieber was spotted in LA wearing a graphic, color-blocked, logo-emblazoned sweater by Martine Rose.

Rihanna is a Martine Rose superfan. In May 2025, she was seen sporting one of the designer’s signature striped polos and baggy-fit jeans on the streets of New York, shortly after revealing her baby bump at that year’s Met Gala.

We’re naturally biased, but one of our favorite Martine Rose moments is without doubt when Billie Eilish graced the cover of our British Vogue’s May 2025 issue, sporting a hot-pink track jacket and headscarf in an updated riff on Balmoral chic.

At the 2025 Super Bowl, Kendrick Lamar—another of Martine Rose’s highest profile superfans—wore a full custom look by the designer for his critically-lauded half-time show, single-handedly reinvigorating the market for denim flares.

In 2025, Timothée Chalamet opted for Martine Rose tailoring for the London premiere of A Complete Unknown, shortly after being spotted in LA wearing one of the brand’s distressed caps.

Kendrick Lamar’s penchant for wearing the brand goes back further than his Super Bowl performance. In 2023, he wore a full look—including a customized track jacket and a then-unreleased colorway of the designer’s viral Nike Shox MR4 mules—to pick up the Grammy for that year’s best rap album.

For further proof of the Biebers’s appreciation for the sportier side of Martine Rose’s offering, look no further than a 2023 Hailey Bieber.

…and here in New York, just a month later.

Rosalía’s appetite for an IYKYK style staple is renowned—as proved by her status as an early adopter of the Nike Shox MR4 in 2022, one of the most hotly coveted products from Rose’s longstanding collaboration with the sports giant.

Proving a Martine Rose track jacket’s irrefutable grail status, Rihanna was repping hers as early as 2022.

#6643. Mamdani and Hochul Visit Queens Night Market to Get Out the Vote

Zohran Mamdani wanted to share with the governor, but the vendor at the Taiwanese Yummy tent wasn’t having it. Cheng Liu insisted the New York mayor try his own bowl of beef noodle soup—the chef’s way.

Instead of trying a bite from Governor Kathy Hochul, Mamdani watched and waited as Liu arranged slippery, wide noodles underneath pickled mustard greens, herbs, and slices of succulent brisket that had been cooked for eight hours, all ladled with a delicate broth. Mamdami started to dig in with his chopsticks when Liu rushed over to spoon in a generous amount of homemade chili oil.

“The mayor is not scared of spicy food,” Liu said via his son’s translation. “We wanted to give him Taiwanese cuisine.”

At the Queens Night Market, Mamdani and Hochul struck an unusual pair: a New York mayor and governor who get along.

Three days before Election Day, the political allies arrived at Flushing Meadows Corona Park in a motorcade of black SUVs to pose for photos and get out the vote for the Democratic party. Hochul has made the city part of her final push in a reelection campaign against Republican Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive endorsed by President Donald Trump.

In a joint interview with Hochul, Mamdani told Bon Appétit that he was showing up for the governor because she was showing up for immigrant New Yorkers. Earlier this year, Hochul signed legislation to ban local and state law enforcement from cooperating with federal immigration operations, and to stop police at all levels from covering their face when interacting with the public.

“The governor has stood up and called for public safety to actually be public safety and not just be an assistance and an accompaniment of ICE,” Mamdani said. “That has been part of what makes people feel like they can be part of this city.”

The mayor also mentioned that the Queens Night Market was a favorite with constituents because of the price. Every dish is capped at $6. Hochul, running on affordability, points to her expansion of free school lunch statewide. “As a mom, this is personal,” she said. “I made a lot of peanut butter and jelly sandwiches over the years for kids.”

Representing different generations and factions of their party, Mamdani and Hochul recognize what they stand to gain together. Mamdani needed Hochul to expand free childcare and greenlight plans for a second-home tax. Hochul needs the enthusiasm of the Democratic Socialist mayor’s voting bloc.

Hochul said she and Mamdani are aligned on lowering the cost of living and supporting the small business owners that make the food and nightlife scene so special.

“It’s a rare day in New York for this kind of relationship,” Hochul said, “but when we talk to each other, we don’t disagree on these issues.”

The pair of politicians approached the night market in a coordinated operation that included advance teams, extra security, and business casual ’fits: Hochul in jeans, Mamdani tie-less in a quarter-zip. The mayor—who has made his appetite a key part of his public identity—appeared less stiff in his interactions with food vendors, but Hochul gamely grabbed chopsticks and posed for selfies.

John Wang, who launched the Queens Night Market in 2015, said politicians are a regular presence here. “Every election season, they come out,” Wang said. “Even if they’ve never been here before, they’re like, ‘Yeahhh! I love the Queens Night Market.’” He said some (2020 presidential candidate Andrew Yang, for instance) get feted like Mamdani, and others (N.Y. Sen. Chuck Schumer) draw a tamer response. Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez used to come a lot, Wang said, and would always get swarmed by supporters.

For the last market of the season, which fell on Halloween, Mamdani might as well have been a member of BTS. Vendors and visitors alike stared slackjawed, squealed, and uttered “oh my God!”

A young man named Asad showed up in a Mamdani costume with no idea he would meet the mayor, let alone pose for photos that brought him to tears.“This is Bruce Blakeman’s nightmare!” the mayor said of his Mamdani double.

“It was surreal, emotional a little bit,” said Asad, who declined to share his last name. Asad said he was born in Karachi, Pakistan, became a U.S. citizen in 2022, and voted for Mamdani after moving to New York from Florida.

At the Ella Spice stand, Akera Phillip represents Grenada with breadfruit croquettes, fried cou-cou, and to-go pouches of sorrel. Phillip, who named her business after her grandmother, felt “elated” and “blessed” to serve her food to the leaders of the state and the city.

“As a small island girl, it just made me feel big,” she said.

Akera Phillip holds breadfruit croquettes.

At the Epis by Steve tent, Hochul told Steve Lahens she could handle “Buffalo spicy,” a nod to her hometown, rather than admit to any trouble with his Haitian pikliz. Lahens and his wife fixed up plates of griot (fried pork) with diri djondjon (black rice) and makawoni au graten, a Caribbean mac and cheese he makes with bell peppers, “evaporated milk and a few little things I can’t talk about.”

Lahens said he was born in Haiti but came to the U.S. in 1988. A workplace injury pushed him toward cooking, “and it changed my life, for the better.” He began cooking out of his house but now works out of the Mangrove shared kitchen at the Flatbush Central Caribbean Marketplace. He was excited to hobnob with the governor and the mayor, but Lahens also said New York small businesses need more help.

“The rent could be lower so people like me could get a spot,” Lahens said. “Right now I’m stuck in catering. I love it, too, but my whole plan and goal is to get a storefront.”

#6642. Spiced Beef Baked Potatoes

Baked potatoes may not seem like a dish that requires much technique, but there’s a difference between a good baked potato and a great one. Wrapping them in foil can lead to a tender interior but render the skin too soft. For the most crisp skin, bake them right on the oven grate at quite a high temperature. (To make it taste almost like a potato chip, rub those scrubbed russets with vegetable oil and season with plenty of salt.) Shockingly, this doesn’t prevent a fluffy interior—that comes down to the internal temperature reaching at least 212°. Sure, it may seem strange to take your potato’s temperature, but it’s a fail-safe route to the most enjoyable potato.

Some, including the Idaho Potato Commission, swear that the way a baked potato is opened affects the texture, eschewing a knife for a fork to gently poke a plus sign into the surface. Others, like beloved food writer Nigel Slater, prefer to strike the potato as though it were part of a martial arts competition. “Bring your hand down fast and sharp as if you were doing a karate chop but only hard enough to crack open the potato skin,” he writes in a piece for The Guardian. (Whether or not to attempt this feat is literally in the hands of the potato-baker.) We found a single fork-pricked line down the length of the spud is the most effective.

Once opened, a baked potato can be filled with anything from tuna salad to cheesy baked beans. Here, it’s a picadillo-inspired mixture with ground beef (packed with protein, iron, and creatine—though ground turkey or chicken work nicely too) adorned with golden raisins and stuffed olives. A spicy tomato sauce will slowly soak into the potato, further seasoning it with every passing minute. Make sure to use a chili powder that’s a mix of spices like chiles, cumin, oregano, garlic (not just dried ground chiles).

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Read more: White Potatoes Are Not Empty Calories. They’re Actually Great for You.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Prick 4 large russet potatoes (about 10 oz. each), scrubbed, patted dry, all over with a fork, then rub all over with 1 Tbsp. vegetable oil and sprinkle with 1¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Bake directly on oven rack until skins are crisp and flesh is very soft (an instant-read thermometer inserted into the center should register 212°–220°), 55–75 minutes. (If thermometer registers 210° before beef mixture is finished, turn off oven and leave potatoes inside until ready to use.)

Meanwhile, pick enough leaves from ½ bunch cilantro (about 2 oz.) to measure ½ cup; set aside for serving. Finely chop remaining leaves and all of stems (you should have about ¾ cup); set aside separately.

Heat remaining 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium. Add 1 medium red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 5 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and cook, stirring occasionally, until onion is softened, 8–10 minutes. Add ¼ cup double-concentrated tomato paste and cook, stirring constantly, until deepened in color and slightly tacky, about 2 minutes.

Increase heat to medium-high. Add 1 lb. ground beef, 2 Tbsp. chili powder, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt. Cook, stirring and smashing often with a heatproof rubber spatula to break up meat, until cooked through, about 4 minutes.

Reduce heat to low. Add ½ cup golden raisins, ¼ cup sliced pimiento-stuffed green olives, reserved chopped cilantro, and 1 cup water. Cook, stirring occasionally, until sauce thickens slightly and flavors come together, 8–12 minutes. Taste beef mixture and season with more salt if needed. Remove from heat and cover. Let sit until ready to use.

Transfer potatoes to a platter or plates and let cool 5 minutes. Using a fork, prick a 3"–4"-long line in the center down length of each potato, leaving 1" unpricked on each end. Using your hands, firmly press ends down toward platter to split potatoes open. Smash flesh as desired, then season inside of potatoes with salt. Divide beef mixture among potatoes and top with reserved cilantro leaves.

#6640. Soho House’s New Tokyo Outpost Is a Maximalist, East-Meets-West Wonder

When the Soho House team first began considering their first-ever Japanese property in 2019, one challenge stood out above all—given their hybrid members’ club with rooms model, the hospitality brand’s Tokyo outpost would need to be all things to all people.

For long-time members touching down in the Japanese capital, it had to deliver a genuine sense of place, immersing them in the city’s creative scene and offering a taste of the local cuisine. For Tokyoites, meanwhile—especially those of an Anglophile persuasion, given Japan’s long-standing reverence for British tailoring, subcultures, and craft—the appeal lay in the opposite direction. With the wealth of exceptional Japanese restaurants and bars already on their doorstep, they’d be looking for a slice of that louche, convivial London clubbiness (and possibly a Sunday roast). On top of that, private members’ clubs are still a relatively foreign concept in Tokyo: the few equivalents that do exist tend to skew more corporate.

It was a tricky square to circle, but if Soho House Tokyo—which opened its doors this summer in the design-forward neighborhood of Aoyama, just a stone’s throw from the frenetic energy of Omotesando crossing—is anything to go by, they’ve pulled it off. Credit belongs in large part to Soho House design director Domhnall Nolan, a self-professed Japan obsessive whose six-year odyssey began before the pandemic hit and involved years of traveling back and forth to study the country’s vernacular architecture, interiors, and craft traditions. “One key thing we honed in on was Soho House being inherently maximalist and Japan having a reputation for minimalism—with Tokyo specifically having that contrast,” Nolan explains. “It’s a city of juxtaposition where you have beautiful moments of calm, and then it’s also extremely dense and chaotic. Everything we were doing was always thinking about that juxtaposition of a minimal detail, but a maximal execution.”

When I arrived a few months back straight off a long-haul morning flight, my brain was still sputtering through the fug of jetlag—though the friendly, laid-back welcome certainly took the edge off. Stepping through the discreet timber double doors off Minami-Aoyama, I discovered a moody, amber-lit reception space wrapped in gridded panels of handmade washi paper and a smart check-in desk swathed in glossy Kyoto lacquer. (Even the staff looked almost absurdly sharp, outfitted in custom Japanese denim uniforms created in collaboration with Onitsuka Tiger; at first glance, they may appear intimidatingly cool, but they’re universally lovely and excited to offer tips for what to check out in the surrounding neighborhood.) The mood, both in the design and the general philosophy, is delightfully irreverent: one corner houses a custom graphic-wrapped Japanese vending machine dispensing striped beach towels, while the walls feature tongue-in-cheek artworks painted to look like oversized Uniqlo and convenience-store receipts. If high design is treated as something of a religion in Tokyo, Nolan clearly wasn’t afraid to commit a little heresy.

From there, I headed up to my bedroom—an “Extra Large” that felt like stepping into the apartment of a well-traveled Tokyo art collector. Passing along corridors lined with further custom washi paper, this time in a shade of indigo inspired by Japanese denim, the doors opened onto a living and dining area bathed in a soothing matcha palette and framed by a wraparound balcony overlooking the Aoyama skyline. (Every single room has a balcony, it turns out—a real rarity here.) The devil is in the details: on a crimson-stained credenza sat a row of Japanese spirits, a cocktail shaker, a ceramic sake set—and, in a delightfully retro touch, a rotary phone. Moving through to the bedroom, a timber bed was dressed with a fringed throw woven from upcycled vintage kimono fabrics in the traditional sakiori style, while the sprawling bathroom featured slabs of striated green marble, speckled Nagoya floor tiles, and a freestanding tub stocked with Cowshed bath salts. Even more thoughtfully, a trio of herbal Ross J. Barr patches had been left out on the table, a lifesaver after my 14-hour flight—I reached for the Sleep variety, stuck them behind my ears, and collapsed onto the immaculate cotton sheets.

That attention to local design extends well beyond the headline suites, however; even the “Cosy” rooms are packed with craft details that are rich with backstory. Nolan tells me later that while putting together a mock-up bedroom back in 2023, he spotted a traditional Japanese jewelry box whose dappled lacquer finish caught his eye, which led him to Makino Urushi, a small family-run workshop in Kyoto. “We went to see their factory, which is a handful of people doing everything themselves,” Nolan recalls. “They have a base of three standard colors—black, gold, and red—and when they show you how they create the other shades, you see the incredible depths of color they get. At one point, someone suggested we could make it cheaper in China, and I said, ‘I’m not going to China to make a Japanese finish.’” That persistence paid off: those intricate dappled lacquer finishes now grace mirror frames and drawer fronts, alongside parquet flooring laid in an interlocking tatami-mat grid.

Anyway, despite slapping on those herbal Sleep Patches, my body clock remained wholly uncooperative. By around 9 a.m., I was still sitting in bed staring out at the foggy Tokyo skyline like Scarlett Johansson in Lost in Translation. Admitting defeat, I headed upstairs to explore the two club floors on the 13th and 14th levels, connected by a monumental timber spiral staircase. Here, Nolan’s East-meets-West tightrope walk is at its most nimble. The so-called Club Lounge is cocooned in glossy burgundy paneling inspired by traditional lacquerware, offset by vintage European and Japanese mid-century armchairs, shelves of vinyl records, and a ceiling paneled with woven sea-grass wallpaper and authentic tatami border trims. “I knew it wouldn’t be appropriate to put actual tatami flooring on the ceiling,” Nolan notes. “There’s a sensitivity to it that Japanese members appreciate.”

My favorite detail? Over at the bar, traditional ceramic roof tiles have been flipped vertically to clad the front counter in a ripple of glazed olive green—an especially wry, witty touch—while the 14th-floor bar pairs glowing Italian Murano chandeliers with handmade lanterns and a swirling ochre-and-green onyx bar top. It’s a lot, but it all comes together to form a pleasing, surprisingly serene whole.

Eventually settling into a low-slung velvet sofa, I ordered the traditional Japanese breakfast: a wooden tray bearing a flaky fillet of grilled salmon, sweet rolled tamagoyaki, sesame-dressed greens on chunky glazed earthenware, and miso soup in a turned wood cup. (It proved to be merely the opening salvo of an extraordinary culinary lineup across the house, but more on that shortly.)

Sufficiently fueled for the day, it was time to brave Aoyama, one of the most dangerous neighborhoods on earth for anyone with a weakness for archival fashion—a category into which, much to the disappointment of my accountant, I very much fall. The surrounding backstreets are a labyrinth of designer flagships and meticulously organized secondhand boutiques; I spent the afternoon darting between three different outposts of the designer resale shop Kindal before wandering through the nearby Issey Miyake mini-district, where the late designer’s sculptural fashion wonders occupy their own string of gallery-like storefronts. (Issey-san’s designs are also significantly cheaper here than in the West, though the stock available can be a little spotty depending on the time of the month.) Eventually, with my jet-lagged limbs about to give way, I walked into Kuu, a nearby Japanese head spa recommended to me by the front desk staff. There, a therapist subjected my scalp, neck, and shoulders to an hour of steam, warm water halos, and pressure-point massage so relaxing I practically sleepwalked back to my room, before collapsing for a catatonic afternoon nap feeling like a freshly steamed dumpling.

That evening, we reconvened for dinner in the private dining room tucked behind frosted glass pocket doors at the far end of the house brasserie. Interestingly, Nolan had originally envisioned an Asian-led concept for the restaurant before pivoting late in the process. “As we looked at everything we had in the house already, we thought, ‘We need something that’s very not Japanese to balance these things out,’” he says. The result is a menu that riffs on British comfort classics using hyper-seasonal Japanese produce: our table groaned under plates of crisp tempura courgette flowers and Yamayuri pork loin glazed in a sweet mead reduction, alongside silver cups of French fries and rounds of spicy Picantes. For pudding, slices of tart topped with jewel-like arrangements of green muscat grapes arrived, alongside coupes of soft-serve ice cream crowned with white miso-infused popcorn—an unpretentious and fabulously umami-rich triumph.

The following morning required an even more brutal wake-up call: a 4:20 a.m. departure for Toyosu Fish Market (an hour that Soho House regulars usually meet on the way to bed, not breakfast) accompanied by Soho House Tokyo’s tuna supplier for backstage access to the morning’s bluefin auction. Pulling up to the recently modernized market complex under a drizzly dawn, we were led through a series of Backrooms-esque corridors before finding ourselves right next to the auction floor, watching dozens of frosted bluefin carcasses lined up on wooden pallets under the fluorescent lights. Buyers in rubber boots moved briskly between the rows, using hooks and flashlights to inspect the fat marbling and ruby-red sheen of each tail cross-section before the rapid-fire hand-signal bidding began. Afterward, we ducked into the wholesale stalls to watch a crew wield sword-length knives to break down the colossal tuna loins with surgical precision—and this exact supply chain made its way onto Chef Shinohara’s sushi counter back at Aoyama hours later, where we enjoyed the tuna with freshly grated Shizuoka wasabi and several pitchers of chilled sake.

After lunch, I spent my final afternoon scoping out the wellness and rooftop spaces. Down on the 13th floor, the dual-zone wellness studio—a jewel box of copper-toned walls, carved timber, and a hand-painted gold ceiling—was in full swing; while the rest of my group admirably threw themselves into a dynamic Reformer Pilates session, after a 4 a.m. fish market excursion, I opted to admire the bespoke leather kettlebells strictly as decorative objects, matcha in hand. Instead, I headed out to the 4,000-square-foot rooftop terrace, where the real showstopper—an infinity-style pool tiled in a geometric grid of bespoke ceramic tiles—looked across the sprawling skyline toward Tokyo Tower. (On a clear day, you can even spot the snow-dusted silhouette of Mount Fuji.)

Sitting by that indigo-tiled rooftop pool as the late-afternoon sun dipped behind the high-rises, my Lost in Translation malaise had been entirely dispelled. In a city that can make even the most seasoned traveler feel like an outsider, Soho House has pulled off something pretty remarkable: a space that honors the rigor of Japanese craft while wrapping you in the heady and ever-so-slightly unruly embrace of a great London club. Another shiso Picante, please.

#6639. A Classic Thanksgiving Menu With Make-Ahead Tips

The editors at Bon Appétit take Thanksgiving very seriously. We are, in fact, in the business of furnishing readers with rigorously tested dishes destined for your family’s annual holiday table (and hopefully—eventually!—the treasured recipe box). What we’ve learned over the years is that—no matter how adventurous a cook might be 364 days of the year—when it comes to T-Day, most people don’t really budge from their traditional mainstays.

People often crave a classic, tried-and-true holiday meal. Guests expect it. So we’re happy to share this menu of Thanksgiving favorites from our archives to get you to the Rockwellian holiday spread of your dreams. These are the dishes we wait all year for: roast turkey and gravy, mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, stuffing, cranberry sauce, buttery rolls, and pumpkin pie. Plus a few tips for making elements ahead.

You’d be hard-pressed to conjure up a more quintessential bird than our 2017 covergirl. This whole-roasted, beautifully burnished Thanksgiving turkey gets a straightforward dry brine, keeping the white meat succulent and juicy.

You can’t beat Andy Baraghani’s make-ahead gravy, which you can prepare up to four days ahead. Reheat it with a bit of stock to revive that perfectly silky texture.

This recipe, originally published as “Ultra-Creamy Mashed Potatoes” in our 2017 Thanksgiving spread, includes its own list of not-to-miss tips for superior mashed potatoes. They’re so good, in fact, they retroactively earned the mantle of BA’s Best. Make sure you know where you’ve stashed the ricer (or food mill).

My colleague Chris Morocco probably didn’t expect his 2016 recipe to become the gold standard for green bean casserole. Yet it’s held that title year after year. No canned cream of mushroom soup here—the savory sauce is totally DIY. The French’s Crispy Fried Onions, however, aren’t going anywhere.

The people have spoken: Victoria Granof’s 2012 stuffing recipe gets virtually dog-eared every Thanksgiving. It’s minimalist but has everything you expect from stuffing (technically “dressing” as it’s cooked outside of the turkey in its own casserole dish), including the quintessential quartet of herbs: parsley, sage, rosemary, and thyme.

Making cranberry sauce is the first order of business on my Thanksgiving menu. I usually whip up a batch of Priya Krishna’s 2019 version the weekend before and feel an outsized sense of pride that I’ve managed to tick one thing off the long prep list. Her recipe is a great starting (or ending) point, but you can jazz it up with a cinnamon stick, star anise, or a few cranks of black pepper if you’d like. Or sub in brown sugar for white—the choice is yours!

Try not to fill up on these buttery treasures before The Big Meal. Originally published in the iconic Fannie Farmer Baking Book, we featured these as part of our 2012 Thanksgiving menu in print. You can bake them ahead of time, let them cool, and keep them in the freezer for reheating. Or, if you’re feeling a little adventurous, try their distant cousin, Salt Bread, for even more oohs and ahhs.

Is it even Thanksgiving without pumpkin pie? Rick Martinez’s 2016 rendition is as classic as they come, and it tastes even better the next day (if you’re lucky enough to have any leftovers… come to think of it, maybe just plan on making two?).

You don’t have to cook the whole menu on Thanksgiving morning. Here’s what you can get out of the way:

Remember to account for oven space on Thanksgiving itself: The green bean casserole still needs baking, the stuffing needs its final uncovered bake, and the rolls need warming.

#6638. Toasted Meringue Hazelnut Blondies

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Lightly coat a 9x9" pan with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Line pan with parchment paper, leaving overhang on two sides. Toast 2 cups blanched hazelnuts on a rimmed baking sheet, tossing halfway through, until golden brown and fragrant, 15–18 minutes. Let sit until cool enough to handle, then coarsely chop; set aside.

Cook 1 cup (2 sticks) unsalted butter in a small saucepan over medium heat, stirring often, until butter foams, then browns (do not burn), 7–9 minutes. Remove from heat.

Whisk 2 large eggs, room temperature, 1 large egg yolk, room temperature, 1¼ cups (250 g) granulated sugar, ¼ cup (packed; 50 g) light brown sugar, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ¾ tsp. instant espresso powder (if using) in the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the whisk attachment on medium-high speed until mixture is pale and doubled in volume, 6–9 minutes (mixture will form an unbroken ribbon when whisk is lifted from bowl).

Reduce speed to low and with motor running, gradually pour in brown butter in a thin, continuous stream; beat until incorporated, about 2 minutes. Remove bowl from mixer and gently fold in 1½ cups (187 g) all-purpose flour with a rubber spatula, scraping down sides and bottom of bowl, until no large, dry streaks of flour remain. Scrape batter into prepared pan; smooth surface. Top with reserved hazelnuts and press in gently to adhere (surface will be smothered with nuts).

Bake blondie until edges are golden brown and center is just set, 35–45 minutes. Transfer pan to a wire rack and let blondie cool in pan. Using parchment paper to help, lift blondie out of pan and transfer to rack.

Meanwhile, combine 3 large egg whites and 1 cup (200 g) granulated sugar in the clean bowl of stand mixer and set over a saucepan of just simmering water (make sure bottom of bowl does not touch water). Heat, whisking constantly, until sugar is dissolved and an instant-read thermometer registers 170°.

Fit bowl onto mixer fitted with clean whisk attachment. Beat egg white mixture until thick and glossy and mixture is barely lukewarm, 8–10 minutes. Add 1 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt; fold in with a rubber spatula just to combine. Taste meringue and season with more kosher salt if needed

Peel away parchment paper from blondie and transfer to a heatproof platter. Using an offset spatula, spread meringue evenly over blondie, covering from edge to edge. Using a kitchen torch, toast meringue until deep golden brown. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Using a long knife and wiping off with a damp kitchen towel between cuts, slice blondie into 9 squares.

Do Ahead: Blondie can be baked 24 hours ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

#6637. Giblet Gravy

Giblets may not be your go-to ingredient just yet, but this Thanksgiving, they just might steal the show. Giblets are the edible offal meat of the turkey, typically the liver, heart, gizzards, and neck, that come in a small paper or plastic pouch stuffed inside the cavity of the bird. Adding them to your traditional gravy brings a depth of flavor that takes this classic side to the next level.

This gravy will also make your life a lot easier during Thanksgiving Day—you can make it while the turkey is still in the oven. It also means you'll be able to use every part of the turkey, and you don't have to throw out that little plastic bag that comes along with your bird. We love a zero-waste recipe!

Start by removing the liver from the giblets and chilling in the refrigerator until you are ready to use.

In a large saucepan over medium heat, combine the rest of the giblets, neck, onion, carrot, garlic cloves, sage, thyme, rosemary, and broth. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce heat, cover, and let simmer very gently for 1 ½ hours.

Add the chilled liver to the broth and simmer until cooked through, which should take an additional 25 minutes.

Strain the broth and discard the remaining neck and all veggies. You should have about 2 ½ cups stock at this point. Afterward, finely chop all giblets and set them aside.

Melt butter in another large saucepan over medium heat. Slowly whisk in the flour and cook until bubbling and just beginning to turn golden, which should take approximately 2 to 3 minutes.

Whisk in ½ cup of strained giblet stock into the gravy at a time, waiting for the ingredient to fully incorporate into the mixture before adding any more.

Once all stock is in, let the gravy simmer while mixing constantly and scraping the bottom of the pot until thickened. This step should take approximately five minutes. Season with salt and pepper and add chopped giblets back into the pot. You’re now ready to serve!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

This gravy can be smothered on turkey, spooned over stuffing and mashed potatoes, or any roasted veggies, but if you have any left over (though we doubt you will), this is the perfect sauce for a leftovers sandwich or for a chicken dinner a couple of days later. Store in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 1 week.

In two new surveys, U.S. adults report lying to their doctors and their children's doctors about symptoms in hopes of being prescribed antibiotics.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly 30% of U.S. adults have lied to doctors in an effort to obtain antibiotics, either by exaggerating their actual symptoms or by fabricating symptoms, the results of a new national survey suggest. Additionally, in a second survey, about one-quarter of children's caregivers reported lying about their kids' symptoms to get antibiotics on their behalf.

"As clinicians, we know that patients lie to us sometimes," Dr. Jeffrey Linder, a general internist and primary care clinician-investigator at Northwestern Medicine, wrote in a commentary about the survey findings.

However, the results are still important because the inappropriate use of antibiotics can contribute to the mounting problem of antibiotic resistance, in which bacteria build up a tolerance to the drugs designed to kill them. Recent data released by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) highlight the extent of the problem: In 2023, drug-resistant bacteria and fungi caused about 9.7 million infections in the U.S., up from 2.8 million in 2017. In turn, the estimated number of deaths caused by drug-resistant germs rose from 35,000 to 50,800 between the two years.

A major factor driving resistance among bacteria is the misuse of antibiotics — in other words, using antibiotics for ailments like viral infections, which the drugs do not treat. For individual patients, such prescriptions don't cure their illness and can result in an upset stomach or issues with the gut microbiome, the community of microbes in the intestines. Simultaneously, they place extra pressure on bacteria to evolve resistance, granting the germs opportunities to pick up new strategies for thwarting antibiotics.

Doctors play a big role in ensuring that the antibiotic prescriptions they write are necessary. Part of their decision-making process comes down to what patients say about their symptoms, some of which may be fabricated, the two new surveys suggest.

The new surveys were published Friday (Oct. 30) in the journal JAMA Network Open.

The first survey was completed by nearly 960 adults from across the U.S. in January and February 2026. It asked whether the respondents had ever told a healthcare provider that their symptoms were worse or more long-lasting than they were in order to get antibiotics, as well as whether they'd ever made up symptoms for the same reason. It then inquired about what motivated a given patient to lie — or avoid lying, if they were truthful — as well as posed contextual questions about their demographics, health behaviors and beliefs.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Overall, about 28% of the respondents reported misrepresenting their symptoms, including 26% who exaggerated their existing symptoms and 17% who fabricated symptoms. They most frequently lied about cold-like symptoms, such as fever, cough and sore throat. About two-thirds of these patients were at least moderately confident that their lie would motivate a clinician to prescribe them antibiotics, and 77% said the strategy worked for them at least once.

Often, patients' motivations for lying centered around feeling very sick, holding strong beliefs that antibiotics would help them recover quickly and get back to their responsibilities, and wanting control over the treatments prescribed to them. Compared with people who didn't lie, those who lied were also more likely to feel that clinicians didn't take them seriously or more likely to endorse statements suggesting that antibiotic resistance is a hoax.

"Greater antibiotic knowledge and aversion to taking antibiotics were associated with lower odds of misrepresentation," meaning lying about symptoms, the study authors noted.

Less than 30% of these patients regretted their lies or taking the antibiotics prescribed to them. Those that did express regret noted experiencing side effects, noticing that the treatment didn't help or feeling that the lying itself was morally wrong.

The second survey was much smaller; it included 236 parents and other guardians of children and teens under 18 years old. It posed similar questions but asked whether the caregivers had lied about their children's symptoms and, if so, what motivated them to lie.

About 27% reported lying about a child's symptoms to get antibiotics, with 87% of these caregivers believing that their lying worked at least once. Their reasons for lying were very similar to those expressed by the respondents in the first survey.

"These findings suggest that symptom misrepresentation may contribute to antibiotic overuse in pediatric care," the study authors concluded.

Ideally, antibiotics should be used only when truly needed, to help relieve the pressure on bacteria to gain resistance.

The surveys reached a diverse group of people, including a range of ages, demographics and locations within the United States; however, the respondents were not necessarily representative of the whole U.S. population, the authors noted. The prevalence of lying should therefore be seen as a tentative measure to be checked in future studies, rather than an unbiased, population-level metric, they wrote. It's also possible that not all the respondents who lied disclosed that they did so or remembered that they had done so.

Especially in outpatient settings, which account for most antibiotic use among U.S. patients, it can be difficult for doctors to quickly determine whether a patient needs an antibiotic.

One factor is that there's a lack of fast, surefire diagnostic tests for many bacterial infections. Outpatient appointments are also extremely short, so doctors sometimes worry about overlooking an infection that could then get worse, Julia Szymczak, a medical sociologist at the University of Utah School of Medicine, previously told Live Science. Another major factor is that clinicians can face pressure to prescribe antibiotics from their adult patients or from children's caregivers, as the new surveys reflect.

But in the face of these pressures and patients' occasional lies, Linder argues that it's still up to the clinicians to do the right thing. "While clinicians might interpret patients' symptom maximization and questions as demands for antibiotics, symptoms do not determine the indication, a diagnosis does," he wrote in the commentary.

"It does not track that approximately 80% of respondents who reported misrepresenting their symptoms obtained a prescription," he added, "unless prescribers were being willfully deceived or, more likely, just getting worn down with what they perceive as patient demand, regardless of actual clinical appropriateness."

When it comes to making decisions about individual patients, Linder argued that doctors don't necessarily need to think about the big picture of antibiotic resistance and how their patient's case fits into that global trend. Rather, providers should simply ask whether a given prescription is more likely to help or hurt that patient, he said.

"Clinicians' obligation is to act in patients' best interest," he said, "even if patients are hoping we do something different, even if patients do not like it, or even if patients lie about their symptoms."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Nicoletta Lanese is the health channel editor at Live Science and was previously a news editor and staff writer at the site. She is a recipient of the 2026 AHCJ International Health Study Fellowship, with a project focused on antibiotic stewardship practices in Japan and the U.S. They hold a graduate certificate in science communication from UC Santa Cruz and degrees in neuroscience and dance from the University of Florida. Beyond Live Science, Lanese's work has appeared in The Scientist, Science News, the Mercury News, Mongabay and Stanford Medicine Magazine, among other outlets. Based in NYC, she also remains involved in dance and performs in local choreographers' work.

#6635. Frico'ed Brussels Sprouts

A slick of oil and a sprinkling of salt are the only adornments brussels sprouts need to shine. But put a crispy Parmesan skirt on them and suddenly the humble veggie becomes the belle of the ball. This recipe does just that. By roasting the brussels sprouts snuggled into a blanket of grated Parmesan cheese, the cheese melts into a crispy, frico-like sheet that clings onto the sprouts, surrounding them in a lace-like halo. It’s a dramatic side dish, but one that makes a serious statement. If roasted correctly, and the stars align in your favor, you can peel off the entire sheet in one swift swoop, presenting it as the culinary masterpiece it is. Fans of fun, this is for you.

It’s That Simple is our series about recipes so easy, you can make them with your eyes closed. Think tiny ingredient lists, laid-back techniques, and results so delicious you’ll text home about them. Read more: Your Brussels Sprouts Need a Crispy, Cheesy Skirt.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a baking sheet with a nonstick baking mat or a sheet of parchment paper generously coated with nonstick vegetable oil spray. Toss 1½ lb. brussels sprouts, trimmed, halved, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper in a medium bowl to combine. Scatter 4 oz. store-bought grated Parmesan (pre-grated works better here than grating from a block) in an even layer over baking sheet, leaving a ½" border around edges. Arrange brussels sprouts, cut side down, in a single layer on top, spacing evenly to fill baking sheet. Bake until brussels sprouts are tender and browned and cheese is deep golden, 20–28 minutes. (If the cheese in the very center is browned, it’s done.) Let cool at least 5 minutes, then break into pieces to serve. (Or place another parchment-lined baking sheet upside down on top; holding together, swiftly turn over, peel away mat, and present cheese side up.)
